1331.title: Block close: the last page
1331.hook: the Bible begins in a garden and ends in a garden-city
1331.howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 1–3 and Revelation 21–22 together as the Bible's bookends, and some churches read the closing chapters of Revelation in the season after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, watchful: lamps lit, and a master who serves. Your line was ready, not afraid.

Bookends hold a row of books upright, one at each end. Read the Bible that way. At the front: a garden, a river, a tree of life, and two people sent out of it, the way back closed behind them. At the back: a river again, and the tree of life again, but now the river and the tree stand in the middle of a city, and the gates are open. A river, a tree, a different place. Everything else sits between them.
screen: `A GARDEN AT THE FRONT, A CITY AT THE BACK.`
`A RIVER, A TREE, A DIFFERENT PLACE.`

segments.voice: First, the garden. Genesis says God planted it, with "the tree of life also in the midst of the garden," and "a river went out of Eden to water the garden." The man is put there "to dress it and to keep it." Then the break: the man and woman are sent out, and the way to the tree of life is guarded, as this block saw beside the healing leaves. Second, the city. Revelation's last chapter shows "a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal," and in the street of the city, on either side of the river, "was there the tree of life." And: "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city." The guarded way is open. Third, why a city and not just the garden again? Some readers notice that the story doesn't rewind. A city is where people live together: streets, gates, neighbors, work. And work is there at both ends. The garden had to be dressed and kept; in the city, "his servants shall serve him." The ending keeps the garden at its heart and wraps human life around it. Fourth, this block, looking back: Revelation as an unveiling, from the Alpha and Omega on Patmos through the throne room and the slain Lamb to Babylon's fall and a wedding feast. Then a new heaven and a new earth, and Christian hope up close, from memento mori and the art of dying, through a seed in the ground and grief with hope, to a lamp kept burning.
screen: `FROM UNVEILING TO A LAMP KEPT BURNING.`

segments.voice: Let a city come to mind, the one you live in or one you love: its streets, its people going to work. Set a river down the middle of the main street, clear as crystal, with a tree on either bank, and keep the shops, the buses, the neighbors. If you pray, hold that picture before God; if you don't, simply stay inside it for a minute.
Block close. The end of this block on Revelation and Christian hope, at the Bible's last page.
Your line: from garden to city. Tomorrow, a new block: rites, spaces and the arts of church life. I'll be here tomorrow.

1332.title: Why rites
1332.hook: rites are patterns of worship that carry memory in bodies
1332.howItsDone: Christians worship through rites such as baptism and the Lord's Supper, and many churches also kneel, stand, bow, raise hands or make the sign of the cross at set points in a service; how much pattern a church keeps varies widely.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page: a garden at the front of the Bible, a city at the back. Your line was from garden to city.

A cake comes out of a dark kitchen with candles burning. Somebody starts a song, and everyone joins on the second note. The birthday person leans in, makes a wish, and blows. Nobody hands out instructions or explains what the candles mean. Hands clap at the right moment anyway, because they've done this before, and somebody did it for them. That little pattern holds years of birthdays inside it. A new block begins here: church life, its rites, spaces and arts. And it starts with a question: why do Christians worship in patterns at all?

A rite is a pattern of worship you do, not just say: words, yes, but also bread, water, standing, kneeling, walking forward. The Bible is full of them. Start with a question a child asks. In Exodus, God tells Israel how to keep the Passover, and adds: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The rite comes first. The question comes later, from a small person at the table who has watched it happen. Jewish families still keep that night, and a child at the table still asks. Next, a meal at that same feast. Luke tells how Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." Do. Not think about, not agree with. Do. Christians still keep that meal, in many shapes, and the coming days walk through several of them. Third, the body joins in. Paul writes, "For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father." A psalm says, "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD." Knees and hands are part of the prayer. Churches differ on how much pattern they keep. Some are rich with it: incense, processions, the sign of the cross. Others keep it plain on purpose, and some keep almost none. Even a plain church tends to have its own way of doing things that newcomers notice right away. A tired mind can forget a sermon. Knees that have bent in the same place for years carry something too. Hands remember where to go.
screen: `A PATTERN YOU DO, NOT JUST SAY.`

segments.voice: Look for a pattern you repeat without thinking: the first cup of the day, a goodnight said the same way, a grave you visit and what you do there. Walk through one slowly in your mind, notice what your hands do, and ask who taught it to you. If you pray, bring that pattern to God and give thanks for whoever started it.
Rite. Worship done with the body as well as said: bread broken, water poured, knees bent.
Your line: bodies remember. A pattern can hold what words let slip. See you tomorrow.

1333.title: The baptism rite
1333.hook: water, oil, a white garment, a lit candle, and a name
1333.howItsDone: Christians baptize with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches add anointing with oil, a white garment and a lit candle, while other churches keep the rite to water and words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rite: worship done with the body as well as said. Your line was bodies remember.

Five things on a small table near the font: a pitcher of water, a little vessel of oil, a folded white cloth, a tall candle already burning, and a card with a name on it. A family holds a baby who has no idea what's coming. Or it's a grown woman in a white robe at the edge of a pool, shaking a little. In the Catholic and Orthodox rites, and in some others, all five things show up. In other churches it's water and a name, and nothing more. Either way, it's the rite that starts a Christian life.
screen: `A BABY, OR A GROWN WOMAN AT A POOL.`

segments.voice: Back in year one, this path looked at when churches baptize, infants or believers, and why. Today is about what the rite does with its hands. First, the water, at the center of every version described here. Paul says the person going under joins Jesus in his death and comes up with him: "buried with him by baptism into death," so that "we also should walk in newness of life." Some churches plunge the whole body, some pour, some sprinkle. The picture underneath is the same. Second, the name. Often a minister asks the parents, or the person, what name they give, and says it aloud over the water. Isaiah has God say to Israel, "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." A name spoken in front of everyone, tied to a promise. Third, the white garment. Paul writes, "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Put on, like clothes. So in some churches the newly baptized are dressed in white, or a white cloth is laid on the baby. The clothes say what the water did. Fourth, the candle. Often it's lit from a larger candle that stands for the risen Christ, and handed to the family. Jesus told his followers, "Ye are the light of the world." Paul writes, "ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord." So the rite ends with a flame in a parent's hand, and a job: keep it going.

Light a candle, or a lamp, or just hold a hand open, for your baptism if you were baptized, or your birth if you weren't. Say your own name quietly, and think of who was there at the start: the people who held you, named you, hoped for you before you could hope anything. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if not, hold them in mind while the light burns.
The baptism rite. Water, a name, a white garment, a candle: the things a church uses to mark the start of a Christian life.
Your line: clothed in light. Put on like a coat, and kept burning. Go gently.

1334.title: Chrismation and confirmation
1334.hook: the Orthodox anoint babies right after baptism; many Western churches confirm in youth
1334.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians are anointed with chrism, chrismation, in the same service as baptism, even as infants; Catholics and some other Western churches confirm later, with the laying on of hands and, in Catholic practice, anointing with chrism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baptism rite: water, a name, a white garment, a candle. Your line was clothed in light.

An old prophet walks into Bethlehem carrying a horn full of oil. He's come to the house of a man named Jesse to find a king. One son after another is brought before him, tall, strong, impressive, and each time the answer is no. Is there anyone else? Well, the youngest. He's out with the sheep. They send for him, and the boy comes in from the field. "Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Oil on the head, and the Spirit comes.
screen: `A PROPHET WITH A HORN OF OIL.`

segments.voice: Chrism is oil set apart for anointing. In Orthodox and Catholic practice it's olive oil with fragrance mixed in, blessed by a bishop. It's the oil of the step that follows baptism, and here the churches split on timing. Orthodox Christians anoint right away. A baby comes up out of the water and, in the same service, the priest touches the oil to forehead, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, chest, hands and feet, saying the words of the rite: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. They call it chrismation. The baby is then a full member, and can come to the table. In the West, Catholics, and some Anglicans and Lutherans among others, usually separate the two. A child is baptized as a baby and confirmed years later, often by a bishop, who lays on hands and anoints with chrism. They call it confirmation. Some other Protestant churches keep a confirmation without oil, as a time to learn the faith and say yes to it, and some have no such rite at all. Both ways point back to the same pages. In Acts, Peter and John come to new believers who had been baptized, and "laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Paul packs it into two verses: God "hath anointed us," and "hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." A seal was pressed into wax to say: this belongs to someone, and it's been closed with care. Same oil. Different clocks.

Touch a little oil or lotion to the inside of your wrist, or just press two fingers there, where you can feel your pulse. Notice the smell, if there is one, and the beat under your fingers. If you pray, say Paul's words slowly, anointed, sealed; if not, keep your fingers on your pulse and count a few beats.
Chrism. Blessed, fragrant oil, used to anoint and seal: right after baptism for the Orthodox, at confirmation for some Western churches.
Your line: sealed. In the old picture, a seal means kept with care, not locked away. Until tomorrow.

1335.title: First communion
1335.hook: a child's first time at the table, remembered for life
1335.howItsDone: Catholic children usually receive first communion in childhood after a period of preparation, often in a parish celebration; Orthodox Christians receive from infancy; Protestant churches differ, some after confirmation, some when a child can understand, some at any age after baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chrism: blessed oil, the same oil on different clocks. Your line was sealed.

A line of children walks up the aisle, two by two. Some girls in white dresses, a few with veils that keep slipping. Boys in shirts buttoned to the top, which they'll undo the second this is over. Grandparents twisting around in the pews with phones up. Each child has practiced this: hands held a certain way, the right answer to say. Then one small girl reaches the front, and it isn't practice anymore. A piece of bread the size of a coin, and a word spoken just to her. Years later she might not remember the homily. She'll probably remember the dress.
screen: `A LINE OF CHILDREN, TWO BY TWO.`
`A PIECE OF BREAD, THE SIZE OF A COIN.`

segments.voice: First communion means a child's first time receiving the bread, and in some churches the cup, at the Lord's table. When depends on the church. In Catholic parishes, a child is usually baptized as a baby and receives first communion later in childhood, after classes, often with a family celebration. The Orthodox do it differently. As yesterday showed, an Orthodox baby is baptized and anointed in one service, and can receive communion right away, a tiny spoonful of bread and wine. So a child raised Orthodox won't remember a first communion; there was never a time they weren't at the table. Protestant churches vary. Some wait until a child is confirmed, some until a child can say what the meal means, and some welcome any baptized child. Each way has a page it leans on. Those who wait often point to Paul: "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup." Those who welcome the very young often point to Mark. People bring little children to Jesus, and the disciples tell them off. "But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Underneath both, a psalm: "O taste and see that the LORD is good." Taste: a mouth, a piece of bread, a first time. Each of these churches is trying to do right by that taste, and they disagree, in earnest, about when.
screen: `A CHILD'S FIRST TIME AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Let one first time come back to you: a first communion if you had one, a first meal in a new home, the first time someone let you sit at the grown-ups' table. Go slowly: what you wore, who was near, what it tasted like. If you pray, thank God for the person who brought you to that table; if you don't, just thank them in your mind.
First communion. A child's first time at the Lord's table, which comes at different ages in different churches.
Your line: the first taste. O taste and see, the psalm says. That's today, done.

1336.title: The Divine Liturgy
1336.hook: the Orthodox service, much of it from Chrysostom's time, sung start to finish
1336.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians gather on Sundays for the Divine Liturgy, usually the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, which is chanted or sung throughout; worshipers often stand, light candles, venerate icons and receive communion at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, first communion, and how churches differ on when a child first comes to the table. Your line was the first taste.

Smoke from a censer, drifting up past painted faces of saints. Candles everywhere. Hardly any pews; people stand. A choir you can't quite see holds one long chord. Then a deacon comes out through a door in the icon screen, carrying a heavy gold-covered book held high. Before the readings he sings out a short call, loud enough to wake anyone drifting off: Wisdom! Let us attend! Everyone straightens. This is the Divine Liturgy, the Sunday service of Orthodox Christians, and nearly all of it is sung.

First, the name. Liturgy is the church's word for worship offered together. Divine, because Orthodox Christians understand it as heaven's worship, joined for a while on earth. The service used most Sundays carries the name of Saint John Chrysostom, a preacher of the early church; tradition credits him with shaping it. Second, it's sung. Nearly every line is chanted or sung, by priest, deacon, choir and people, back and forth. The deacon calls out a petition, for peace, for the sick, for travelers, and the people answer each one: Lord, have mercy. The answer stays the same while the needs change. Third, the movement. Twice the clergy come out in procession: first with the gospel book, the little entrance; later with the bread and wine, the great entrance, while the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn, which asks the people to lay aside all earthly cares. Then, as the bread and wine are offered, the people sing a hymn built on the song the prophet Isaiah heard the seraphim singing: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as joining the angels' worship. Fourth, the call. Again and again the deacon says it: Wisdom, let us attend. Before the readings, before the creed, before the gifts. It isn't decoration. It's a wake-up call for a mind that wanders, sung over and over, because minds wander over and over.

If you can, play a recording of the Divine Liturgy, or any old church music sung by voices, quietly; if not, listen to the room around you. Don't try to follow the words; each time your mind wanders, don't scold it, just say inside, let us attend, and come back to the sound. If you pray, you can join the old answer: Lord, have mercy.
The Divine Liturgy. The Sunday service of Orthodox Christians, sung nearly from start to finish, which carries the name of John Chrysostom and comes to the table near its end.
Your line: let us attend. Sung by a deacon, kept by anyone. See you tomorrow.

1337.title: The shape of the Mass
1337.hook: gathering, word, table, sending: the Catholic path walks it slowly
1337.howItsDone: Catholics attend Mass on Sundays and holy days; it moves through introductory rites, the Liturgy of the Word, the Liturgy of the Eucharist and the concluding rites, ending with a blessing and a dismissal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Liturgy, sung nearly start to finish. Your line was let us attend.

Two friends are walking from Jerusalem to a village at the end of a terrible weekend. A stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're talking about. They tell him everything: their teacher, the cross, the empty tomb nobody can explain. And the stranger starts at Moses and walks them through the scriptures, mile after mile. At the village they beg him to stay. He sits down to eat with them, takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. In that moment they know who he is. The Mass walks a shape much like that road.

The Catholic Mass has four movements; the church's own books lay it out that way. First, gathering. People come in from separate lives: a procession, a song, the sign of the cross, and a moment to admit what's gone wrong this week, answered with Lord, have mercy. Strangers become a congregation. Second, the word. Readings from the Old Testament, a psalm, a letter, and then everyone stands for the gospel. A homily opens it up. It's the road to Emmaus again, where the friends said afterward, "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" Third, the table. Bread and wine are brought forward. The priest prays the great prayer of thanksgiving and repeats the words of Jesus over them, and the people come forward to receive. Catholics believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. At Emmaus, "he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him." Fourth, sending. A blessing, and the people are sent out. The old Latin dismissal says, Ite, missa est. Roughly, it means go, it is the dismissal, and many hear in it, go, you are sent. Tradition says the word Mass comes from it. The service doesn't so much end as push you out the door. The friends went the same way: "they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem." Gather, hear, eat, go. Once the four are clear, they turn up in other churches too.

Walk the four parts slowly: gather, letting the scattered pieces of your day come in and sit down; hear, bringing back one line that's stayed with you this week; the table, remembering the last meal you shared and who sat across from you. Then go: picture the next place you'll walk into. If you pray, offer each part to God as you go.
The shape of the Mass. Four movements: gathering, the word, the table, and sending.
